title: Review: Classification and cladistics; Evolution and speciation; Conservation of biodiversity; Carbohydrates and lipids
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for IB Diploma Biology (review status in the bank: ai-specialist-reviewed-gate-verified-2026-09-21-awaiting-human-signoff). assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Species richness
items.clue: The number of different species present in a community or area.

items.label: Evolution
items.clue: Change in the heritable characteristics of a population over generations.

items.label: Speciation
items.clue: The splitting of a pre-existing species into two or more species that can no longer interbreed.

items.label: Over-exploitation
items.clue: Harvesting a species faster than its population can replace itself, by hunting, fishing or collecting.

questions.stem: Which of these changes would a biologist regard as evolution?

options.text: The frequency of an allele for dark wing colour rises in a moth population over many generations.
The muscles a weightlifter enlarges by training are inherited by the weightlifter's children.
An individual Arctic fox grows a thicker and whiter coat each year as winter approaches.
Young chimpanzees learn from adults how to crack nuts with stones, and the skill spreads.

questions.stem: For one gene, two species have identical amino acid sequences in the protein, yet the base sequences of the gene differ at six positions. Which statement explains this?

options.text: They are not evidence of divergence, because they have had no effect on the protein.
The genes must actually be identical, so the six differences are sequencing errors.
Similar environments keep the proteins alike while the DNA of each species drifts apart.
Some base substitutions leave the amino acid that is coded for unchanged.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of speciation?

options.text: A species changes gradually over millions of years until it looks quite different from its ancestors.
A river splits a population into two halves, which are at once regarded as separate species.
An individual is born with a mutation that makes it different from all others of its species.
A population splits into two groups that then become unable to interbreed with each other.

questions.explanation: Speciation is the splitting of a pre-existing species into two or more species that can no longer interbreed. It is the only way in which new species have appeared.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Caribbean monk seal (Neomonachus tropicalis) case study is correct?

options.text: It became extinct only after industrial fishing fleets reached the Caribbean in the twentieth century
It was hunted for the oil in its blubber from the 1490s, an anthropogenic extinction of a marine mammal species
It shows that marine species are otherwise safe, since the open ocean is too large for people to affect them
Its extinction counts as anthropogenic only because seals were killed; the fishing of its prey was a natural pressure

questions.stem: Why do surveys of biodiversity need to be repeated to provide evidence for a biodiversity crisis?

options.text: Repeating a survey is needed only when the first survey was carried out by citizen scientists rather than experts
Repeating a survey finds additional species, and so gives a higher measure of the habitat's biodiversity
A change in species richness or evenness can only be shown by comparing surveys made at two different times
A single thorough survey is sufficient, provided that it covers a wide enough range of habitats around the world

questions.stem: Which factor is the overarching cause of the current biodiversity crisis, driving each of the specific causes?

options.text: Spread of cities over natural habitat
Natural spread of invasive species
Natural climate shifts as in past eras
Growth of the human population

questions.explanation: The guide names human population growth as the overarching cause, with hunting and over-exploitation, urbanization, deforestation and clearance for agriculture, pollution and the spread of pests, diseases and invasive alien species as the specific causes it drives.

questions.stem: Which description of an approach to the conservation of biodiversity is correct?

options.text: Nature reserves conserve species by keeping people out, so no management is needed
Ex situ conservation in zoos can, by itself, secure the future of an endangered animal species
Rewilding restores natural processes to an area, often by reintroducing missing species
Seed banks can store the germ plasm of every plant species by drying and freezing its seeds

questions.stem: A student measures the diameter of a cell as 7 µm. What is this diameter in nanometres?

options.text: 70 nm, because each prefix is ten times the next
7000 nm, because one micrometre is 1000 nanometres
0.007 nm, because a smaller unit means a smaller number
7 000 000 nm, because a micrometre is 10⁻³ of a metre

questions.explanation: 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m and 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, so 1 µm = 1000 nm. The length is unchanged; it is expressed in a smaller unit, so the number is larger: 7 × 1000 = 7000 nm.

questions.stem: Two monosaccharides are joined by a condensation reaction to form a disaccharide. What happens in this reaction?

options.text: A molecule of water is taken in and split to supply the atoms that join the monomers
A hydrogen bond forms between the two monomers, holding them together as a disaccharide
Water dissolves the two monomers so that they meet, but no water is formed or used
A covalent bond forms between the monomers and a molecule of water is released

questions.stem: A polypeptide made of 100 amino acids is completely hydrolysed into free amino acids. How many water molecules are used in the process?

options.text: 99 water molecules
100 water molecules
1 water molecule
0 water molecules

questions.explanation: A chain of 100 amino acids contains 99 peptide bonds. Each hydrolysis reaction breaks one bond and uses one water molecule, which is split to supply the -H and -OH added to the products, so 99 water molecules are used.

questions.stem: Carbon forms an enormous diversity of compounds, on which life is based. Which statement about the bonding of a single carbon atom is correct?

options.text: It forms up to four covalent bonds, single or double, with carbon or other non-metal atoms
It forms any number of covalent bonds, which is why so many carbon compounds exist
It transfers its four outer electrons to other atoms, giving charged compounds
It links to neighbouring carbon atoms by weak hydrogen bonds that are easily broken

questions.stem: Why is the digestion of a polymer into its monomers described as a hydrolysis reaction?

options.text: Water acts only as the solvent in which enzymes break the polymer into its monomers
Water molecules are split, and the -H and -OH produced are added to the monomers
Breaking the bonds between the monomers releases the energy that was stored in those bonds
Water molecules are released as each bond between neighbouring monomers is broken

questions.explanation: Hydrolysis means splitting with water. For each bond broken, one water molecule is split; its -H is added to one product and its -OH to the other, so the water is incorporated into the monomers.

questions.stem: The rRNA base sequences of an archaean are found to differ from those of bacteria as much as they differ from those of eukaryotes. Which classification does this evidence support?

options.text: Archaea placed within the domain Bacteria, since both groups lack a nucleus.
Archaea as a sixth kingdom, the highest level of classification.
Archaea as a separate domain, distinct from both Bacteria and Eukarya.
Archaea grouped with bacteria, because cell structure outweighs rRNA evidence.
